response.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT c.gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), s AS (SELECT gender, order_count, order_count * 1.0 / SUM(order_count) OVER () AS share FROM g), a AS (SELECT gender, order_count, share, AVG(share) OVER () AS avg_share FROM s) SELECT gender, order_count, share, share - avg_share AS share_above_average FROM a WHERE share > avg_share;

assumptions.assumption: An 'invoiced order' is an order with at least one invoice, so an order with several invoices is counted once (COUNT DISTINCT order_id).
The average share is the unweighted mean of the per-gender shares (equal to 1 / number of gender groups), and a NULL gender, if any customer has one, counts as its own group.
Inner joins drop invoices that do not link to an order and customer, as the request says to skip anything that doesn't link up.

alternatives.interpretation: Count invoices rather than distinct orders, so an order with multiple invoices is counted once per invoice.
alternatives.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT c.gender, COUNT(i.invoice_number) AS order_count FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), s AS (SELECT gender, order_count, order_count * 1.0 / SUM(order_count) OVER () AS share FROM g), a AS (SELECT gender, order_count, share, AVG(share) OVER () AS avg_share FROM s) SELECT gender, order_count, share, share - avg_share AS share_above_average FROM a WHERE share > avg_share;
